To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the dust grains along the line of Cyg X2 are smoothly distributed at least for ∝60% of their path to the source, (ii) the scattering halo contributes ∝5–7% of the total source emission in the ∝1−10 keV band, (iii) the halo spectrum is dominated by silicates and the scattering cross section is consistent with the Mie theory, (iv) the absorption by oxygen in the ISM is complex, and

(i) the halo around CygX-2 is well detected and contributes ∼ 5–7% of the total source emission; (ii) in the halo spectrum we detect the signature of dust elements: O, Mg, and Si, and the major contribution comes from silicates; and (iii) the dust is smoothly and uniformly distributed toward the source at least for 60% of the line of sight.

(i) the scattering halo is well detected in the EPIC-pN image of Cyg X−2 and it contributes ∼5% to ∼7% to the source emission at 2 keV, and (ii) the spectral analysis of the scattering halo indicates that the dust is mainly composed by silicates, and that it is smoothly distributed toward the source.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the dust distribution and composition along the line of the sight toward Cyg X2, as well as the dust size distribution in the local ISM.
a new application of the X-ray scattered halo as a probe of the ISM dust properties.
the study of the interstellar medium in the vicinity of the source.

the dust is distributed smoothly toward Cyg X−2 and the dust grain sizes are in the range 0.05−0.2 μm.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dust grains are smoothly distributed in the line of sight and the scattering is dominated by silicates.
the dust grains are well mixed with molecular oxygen and that a large fraction of dust grains is distributed in the line of sight of Cyg X−2.
the dust is distributed smoothly toward Cyg X−2, and that it contains a substantial amount of molecular oxygen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
X-ray spectroscopy of the halo can provide a new and independent method to study the ISM.
XMM-Newton observations of bright X-ray sources are a powerful tool to study the ISM.
XMM-Newton can be used to perform spatially resolved spectroscopic studies of the interstellar scattering halos around bright X-ray sources.
